newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbia makes new effort to fund 1997 wheat sowing.
newsitem.headline: Serbia makes new effort to fund 1997 wheat sowing.

text.p: Serbia's Commodity Reserve Agency on Monday reopened the sale of wheat contracts to finance the 1997 wheat sowing, the Belgrade bourse said.
Two new tranches of wheat contracts maturing August 31, 1997, will be on sale until February 7, the bourse said.
The D3 tranche is worth 49.55 million dinars while the D4 is worth 99 million dinars. The latter can be paid in four instalments, while D3 is payable at once.
The contract's face value is 9,000 dinars, with 10 tonnes of wheat sold as collateral and a 32 percent discount.
Wheat contracts provide the holder with an export licence.

The Commodity Reserve Agency launched D1 and D2 tranches of wheat contracts worth almost 150 million dinars on October 3. The sale was closed on December 2 with a little over 30 million dinars worth of contracts sold.
"This is more of a success than a failure," Goran Altaras, commodities specialist on the Belgrade Stock Exchange, told Reuters.

"If the volume of the Yugoslav financial market stands around 200 million dinars of free funds and you have managed to attract 15 percent of those funds to long-term investment, then it is a success," he said.
Major investors were flour mills and bakeries, he added.
Analysts said they would have bought even more if they had appropriate financial support from the commercial banks.
Banks did not emerge as buyers over the two-month period because tight liquidity did not allow them to commit funds for a period as long as 285 days, they said.
"Any long-term investment on the Yugoslav financial market is bound to fail," an analyst who asked not to be named, said.

In an attempt to reverse the central bank's decision to increase the reserve requirement to 15 from 10 percent, bankers said they would pour 75-80 million dinars into wheat contracts if the central bank reduced the reserve requirement.
Altaras expected flour mills and bakeries to remain key investors.
"Those contracts are attractive for their price, because they sell one kilo of wheat for 0.9 dinars while the same quantity already fetches 1.45 dinars on the spot market," he said.
